title: Check if a string contains only digits (loop through each character, check `Character.isDigit()`).
shortTitle: Check if a String Contains Only Digits

s1_definition.profdef: Checking whether a string contains only digits means verifying that every character in the string is one of the decimal digit characters zero through nine, with no letters, spaces, punctuation, or symbols anywhere. The straightforward approach loops over each character and tests it with `Character.isDigit`, returning false at the first non-digit and true only if the loop completes. This runs in linear time in the length of the string and treats an empty string as not all-digits by convention.
s1_definition.analogy: When Rajesh types his account number or an amount into the National Bank of India app, the system must be sure he typed only numbers and did not slip in a letter or a stray space. The check walks along the typed text one character at a time, and the moment it sees anything that is not a digit it stops and says "not valid". Only if every single character is a digit does it say "this is a clean numeric field".
s1_definition.oneliner: Walk every character, fail fast on the first non-digit, and only pass if the whole string is digits and non-empty.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Checking whether a string contains only digits means verifying that every character in the string is one of the decimal digit characters zero through nine, with no letters, spaces, punctuation, or symbols anywhere. The straightforward approach loops over each character and tests it with `Character.isDigit`, returning false at the first non-digit and true only if the loop completes. This runs in linear time in the length of the string and treats an empty string as not all-digits by convention.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When Rajesh types his account number or an amount into the National Bank of India app, the system must be sure he typed only numbers and did not slip in a letter or a stray space. The check walks along the typed text one character at a time, and the moment it sees anything that is not a digit it stops and says "not valid". Only if every single character is a digit does it say "this is a clean numeric field".

**One line to remember:** Walk every character, fail fast on the first non-digit, and only pass if the whole string is digits and non-empty.

sections.s2_technical:
The simplest reliable method is an explicit loop. You iterate over the characters of the string by index, and for each character you call `Character.isDigit`. The moment one character is not a digit, you return false immediately, which is called failing fast and avoids scanning the rest. If the loop finishes without finding a non-digit, you return true.

An important edge case is the empty string. An empty string has no characters, so a naive loop finishes immediately and would return true, but by banking convention an empty field is not a valid numeric input. So I add an explicit guard that returns false when the string is null or empty.

There is a subtlety with `Character.isDigit` that senior engineers should know. It returns true not only for the familiar ASCII digits but also for digit characters from other scripts, such as Devanagari or Arabic-Indic digits, because it is Unicode-aware. For a bank processing international input this can be surprising. If you want strictly the ASCII digits zero through nine, you compare the character against the range from the character zero to the character nine, or you use a regular expression that matches only ASCII digits.

A concise alternative is a regular expression. The pattern of one or more ASCII digits anchored at both ends checks the whole string in one call. For hot paths I prefer the explicit loop because it avoids the cost of compiling or matching a pattern, and because failing fast is cheap. For readability in non-hot code the regular expression is fine, but I pre-compile the pattern once rather than recompiling it on every call.

A related point is that even when a string is all digits, it may still not fit in an int or long if it is very long, so "all digits" is not the same as "parseable into a number". For amounts I validate digits first and then parse into a BigDecimal, which has no range limit, rather than assuming it fits a primitive.

A small finance-domain example: `boolean allDigits = true; if (s == null || s.isEmpty()) allDigits = false; else for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) { if (!Character.isDigit(s.charAt(i))) { allDigits = false; break; } }` leaves `allDigits` true only for a clean numeric field.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, the account-opening form lets Rajesh type a proposed account number and an initial deposit amount. Before anything reaches the backend, the input layer must reject fields that contain anything other than digits, because an account number with a stray letter or an amount with a hidden space will crash downstream parsing or, worse, be misinterpreted. Validating that a field is only digits is exactly this check.

This is exactly how the all-digits check works in Java — we loop over the typed characters and reject at the first non-digit.

Problem 2 — The bank operates across regions and sometimes receives input containing non-ASCII digit characters that look numeric but are from other scripts, which the parsing library then handles inconsistently. The validation must be strict about ASCII digits only for the account-number field, so the code must offer a stricter variant that rejects non-ASCII digits even though `Character.isDigit` would accept them.

What the code will do: an `InputValidator` class with `isAllDigits(String s)` using `Character.isDigit` with an empty guard, and `isAsciiDigitsOnly(String s)` using an explicit ASCII range check. The demo validates Rajesh's clean account number, a bad amount with a space, and a non-ASCII digit string.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build

# Run the demo
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh types the account number `2001` and a deposit amount `50 000` with a stray space.

Step 1: `isAllDigits("2001")` runs. The string is not null and not empty, so we enter the loop.

Step 2: We check each character. Index zero is `2`, a digit; index one is `0`, a digit; index two is `0`, a digit; index three is `1`, a digit. The loop finishes without finding a non-digit, so the method returns true. The account field is clean.

Step 3: `isAllDigits("50 000")` runs. It is not empty, so we enter the loop. Index zero is `5` and index one is `0`, both digits. Index two is a space, which is not a digit, so we fail fast, log the position, and return false immediately without checking the rest.

Step 4: `isAllDigits` on the Devanagari string containing the characters for one, two, three returns true, because `Character.isDigit` is Unicode-aware and treats Devanagari numerals as digits. This is the surprising case the bank must be careful about.

Step 5: `isAsciiDigitsOnly` on the same Devanagari string returns false, because each character falls outside the ASCII range from the character zero to the character nine. This is the strict variant used for the account-number field.

Step 6: The final results are that the clean account passes, the spaced amount fails, and the Devanagari string passes the Unicode check but fails the strict ASCII check. No input was modified; validation only reads.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T14:50:00Z INFO Rajesh account '2001' all-digits? true
2026-10-26T14:50:00Z INFO Amount '50 000' all-digits? false
2026-10-26T14:50:00Z INFO Devanagari string Unicode all-digits? true
2026-10-26T14:50:00Z INFO Devanagari string ASCII-only digits? false
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: account "2001", amount "50 000", devanagari "१२३"
    │
    ▼
  isAllDigits("2001")
    │ non-empty → scan 2,0,0,1 all digits → true
    ▼
  isAllDigits("50 000")
    │ scan 5,0,[space] → fail fast at index 2 → false
    ▼
  isAllDigits("१२३")  → Unicode digits → true  (surprise!)
  isAsciiDigitsOnly("१२३") → outside '0'..'9' → false
    ▼
  Output: clean account ok, spaced amount rejected,
          strict ASCII guard catches non-ASCII numerals
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
To check whether a string contains only digits, I loop over every character and test each one with Character dot isDigit, returning false the moment I hit a non-digit and returning true only if the whole string passes. This is linear in the length of the string and fails fast, which keeps it cheap on bad input.

The edge case I always call out is the empty string. A bare loop would return true for an empty string because there is nothing to reject, but by convention an empty numeric field is not valid, so I guard null and empty up front and return false.

The senior nuance is that Character dot isDigit is Unicode-aware, so it accepts digit characters from scripts like Devanagari or Arabic-Indic, not just the ASCII zero through nine. For a bank that receives international input this can be surprising and can confuse downstream parsing, so when a field must be strictly ASCII I compare each character against the range from the character zero to the character nine instead. I also remember that "all digits" does not guarantee the value fits in an int or long, so for money I validate digits and then parse into a BigDecimal, which has no range limit.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to validate account numbers and deposit amounts on the onboarding form before anything reached the backend, rejecting fields with stray spaces or letters, and I offered a strict ASCII-only variant for the account-number field so non-ASCII numerals could not slip through. Explaining the Unicode subtlety and the empty-string convention shows the interviewer that I think beyond the happy path, which is exactly what matters when validating real financial input.
